Keywords: You

outputs.L1:
You must understand—sighting that pair of eagles
above the block, directly over our house,
no more than twenty feet above the roofline,
so massive that their wings, even tilted gently,
seem to tug at the corrugated tin below—
this sight counters the bitterness I feel
toward all the damage I witness and hear
on this relentlessly clear, blue morning,
when clarity itself becomes a kind of pain,
and even one small wattle tree, now gone,
utterly vanished since I was last home—
I still find this difficult to say—
is its own private agony;
for a region is not a single point,
and a different compass turns within me,
its needle drawn toward every direction at once,
yet always settling on the one place
I know and watch as closely as I can;
and so even that small, vanished wattle tree
becomes an agony bordering on grief,
where breath itself grows difficult,
where sustaining myself past the loss is hard;
yet still, the eagles reappear,
their sharp and vigilant eyes unwavering,
and this transcends the ordeal—
though I wish life, too, for their prey,
whose suffering is no less real than any other;
this is the whole of the sense, or nonsense,
I can make in such blue and merciless light.

A place isn't just one location; there's another kind of compass guiding my thoughts, one with magnetic pull in every direction, yet all those directions converge on this one spot I'm watching as carefully as I can. # On Eagles and Small Losses

There is a particular kind of morning—clear, crisp, almost merciless in its clarity—when the sight of a pair of eagles flying low over the house becomes something more than ordinary wonder. It arrives as a counterweight, a force pressed against the bitterness that seems to gather at the edges of everything else, the accumulated damage the speaker has come to notice in the landscape they know so intimately. On such mornings, when the light itself seems to sharpen every flaw and absence into painful focus, even something as small as the loss of a single wattle tree—gone since the speaker was last home—takes on outsized weight. It registers not as a minor botanical casualty but as something closer to grief, an ache disproportionate to its cause, almost indistinguishable from mourning a death.

This intensity of feeling speaks to something deeper: an internal orientation the speaker carries, not unlike a compass whose needle has fixed itself, magnetically and irrevocably, toward this one place. It is a home known so closely, watched so carefully over time, that its smallest changes register as seismic. Every missing tree, every subtle shift in the terrain, becomes legible to a mind attuned to this singular landscape in a way that admits no substitute.

And yet, into this heightened state of noticing and grieving, the eagles continue to move—present, unhurried, their eyes keen and watchful in a way that seems to cut through the speaker's private ordeal of loss. Their persistence offers a kind of override, a redirection of attention that does not erase the grief but somehow sits alongside it, tempering it. This is not without its own complication, though: the speaker does not romanticize the eagles without reservation, aware as they are of the trauma such predators inflict upon their prey. The beauty of the birds is inseparable from the violence they represent to whatever creatures fall beneath their gaze.

To hold both of these truths at once—the wonder of eagles overhead and the grief for small, accumulating damages on the ground—is, the speaker admits, a task that resists easy resolution. In this strange, blue-lit moment, where morning light seems to make everything both clearer and stranger, reconciling these feelings produces a result that is neither wholly sensible nor wholly absurd. It hovers somewhere between the two, faithful to the contradictions of a place both loved and altered, both watched over and grieved for, in the same breath.
outputs.L4:
# The Eagles

I saw them yesterday morning, low over the ridge where the old house used to catch the first light—two eagles, wingspan so vast they seemed to drag the sky down with them as they passed. I stood in the yard and did not breathe. It has been years since I have seen anything move through that particular stretch of air with such unhurried authority, such indifference to all that has been lost beneath them.

And so much has been lost. I do not say this lightly, nor do I say it for effect. The wattle tree—the single wattle tree that stood at the bend in the creek, that flowered gold every August without fail, that I climbed as a child and later simply sat beneath, feeling the shade move across my face like something living—it is gone now. Cut, or fallen, or simply erased by whatever slow violence has been working on this land. I cannot say which. I only know that when I went looking for it last spring and found nothing but a stump gone soft and grey with rot, I sat down on the ground right there and wept as though someone had died. Because someone had. Something had. The tree was not merely a tree; it was a marker of time, a thing that measured my life against its own slower one, and now that measure is gone, and I am unmoored in a way that feels disproportionate to a tree, and yet is not disproportionate at all.

This is how the grief works now—not as one great wave but as a thousand small erasures, each one insisting on its own significance, each one a little death I am required to grieve in full before the next arrives. The creek that no longer runs in summer. The paddock gone to weeds no bird will nest in. The silence where there used to be frogs. I have become someone who catalogs absences, who walks the old paths and inventories what is missing the way one might check a pulse.

So when the eagles came—when they came in low and slow and utterly unbothered, riding some current I could not feel from the ground—I did not expect to feel anything but the same familiar ache. I know what they are, after all. I know that even as I watched them, they were likely searching the grass below for something small and warm and alive, that their beauty is inseparable from their hunger, that somewhere in the next hour a rabbit or a lamb would end because of exactly this unhurried grace I found myself so moved by. I have never been able to fully forgive nature for this arrangement, this insistence that survival be built on such intimate violence. It complicates the awe. It always has.

And yet.

Watching them, I felt something shift that I had not expected to shift—a loosening, brief and involuntary, in the grip that grief has held on my chest these past months. There they were: the same birds, or birds enough like them, that must have flown this same low arc over this same ridge when I was a child, when the wattle was young and gold and the creek ran all year. They did not know what had been lost. They did not care. Their eyes—sharp enough, I imagined, to catch the glint of a single beetle from three hundred feet—had no use for my sorrow, no interest in the stump by the creek or the silence in the paddock. They simply flew, as they had always flown, as they would likely continue to fly long after I am gone and the grief along with me.

I do not know if this is comfort, exactly. I am wary of calling it that, wary of the neatness such a word implies. It felt more like a kind of physics—the simple fact of their continuance pressing up against the fact of my loss, neither canceling the other out, but both, for one strange suspended moment, occupying the same sky. The eagles did not fix anything. They did not bring back the wattle or the frogs or the creek's summer voice. But they flew low enough that I could hear, faintly, the sound their wings made against the air, and for that moment the sound was enough. For that moment, something in the world continued, sharp-eyed and indifferent and utterly alive, and I found that I could breathe again, just barely, just enough to keep standing there and watch them go.
outputs.L5:
# You

You are the one reading these words right now. Before them, silence—no sentence had yet reached you, no thought had crossed this particular bridge between mind and page. And yet here you are, transforming ink and pixels into meaning, into something that lives, however briefly, inside your own awareness.

There is something strange about the word "you." It is the most personal pronoun and yet the most universal. Every person who has ever lived has been someone's "you"—a child called by a parent, a friend addressed across a table, a stranger acknowledged with a nod. The word never refers to itself; it always points outward, toward another consciousness, another center of experience separate from the speaker's own.

To be a "you" is to be recognized. It means someone else has paused, has turned their attention toward you, has decided that you matter enough to be spoken to directly. Compare this to being spoken *about*—to being a "they" or a "someone." When you are addressed as "you," you are drawn into relationship. You cannot ignore it the way you might ignore a fact stated in the abstract. Second person address demands something from you: attention, response, presence.

Philosophers have long puzzled over the nature of the self implied by "you." Martin Buber famously distinguished between "I-It" relationships, where we treat others as objects to be used or observed, and "I-Thou" relationships, where we meet another being in their full subjectivity. Every genuine "you" carries this Thou-quality—an acknowledgment that behind the name, behind the face, there is an inner world as real and complex as your own.

And yet you are also mysterious to yourself. What does it mean when you turn the word inward, when you ask yourself, "What do you want?" or chastise yourself with "You should have known better"? In these moments, the self splits into observer and observed, speaker and listener, as if we each contain multitudes and must occasionally negotiate between them.

Every story ever told about "you" is really a story about being seen—being called into existence by another's attention, being invited into dialogue, being reminded that you are not alone in this strange business of consciousness looking out at the world.

So here, now, this text ends by turning back to you: not as an abstraction, not as anyone in general, but as the specific person holding this moment in your hands. What will you do with it?

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about seeing a pair of eagles over your childhood home while grappling with grief over environmental loss and a missing wattle tree.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Eagles Saw**

Two eagles the size of my grief
turn slow circles over the gully,
wingtips spread like fingers reading braille
in the wind. I stand where the driveway
crumbles into gravel, remembering
this was not always so quiet.

There was a wattle here—
I want to say exactly where,
but the ground has closed over it
like water over a dropped stone.
Now only grass gone the color
of old newspaper, and a fence post
leaning the way old men lean
when they've stopped waiting for anything.

Every August it went off like a flare,
that tree, a small sun caught in branches,
pollen thick enough to make my mother sneeze
on the back step, bees so drunk on it
they forgot to fear us.
I'd rub the flowers between my palms
just to carry the smell into the house,
into sleep, into every room
I ever loved.

The eagles bank against a sky
the color of a bruise healing wrong.
They don't know what's missing.
They only know the thermals still rise here,
the gully still breathes enough warm air
to hold them up. Maybe that's what survival is—
not remembering, just still finding
enough lift to stay aloft
over what's been taken.

I drove four hours to stand
in a place that no longer needs me
to recognize it. The house is not the same color.
The dog has been dead longer than it lived.
But the eagles keep circling true,
marking this ground as worth returning to,
even as I stand here
trying to recall
which precise handful of dirt
once held something
that could not be replanted—
only mourned,
only carried, pollen-light,
in the closed fist of memory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a long-lined, run-on style poem about the tension between awe at nature's predators and mourning for their prey and vanished landscapes.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Hawk Knows and What the Field Forgets**

I have stood at the lip of a ravine and watched a red-tailed hawk unstitch the afternoon,
its shadow dragging over stubble and stone like a rumor no one wanted to believe,
and felt something in my chest lift too, some ancient animal gladness at the folding of wings,
at the moment of plummet when the whole sky seems to exhale through a single body,
and I have called this beautiful, have used that word without apology, have stood there
grinning like the descendants of prey are allowed to grin at the machinery of their undoing,
because it is not my undoing, not today, not in this century, and so I can afford
the luxury of awe, can afford to watch the field mouse become an afterthought,
a small brown punctuation mark at the end of a sentence written in feathers and need—

and still, and still, some other part of me keeps score, keeps a ledger of the diminishing,
counts the rabbits that no longer start from the hedgerows because the hedgerows are gone,
counts the antelope herds thinned to anecdote, to grainy footage, to the museum diorama
where the lion crouches forever mid-leap over a gazelle that will never finish falling,
both of them taxidermied into an eternal present tense that pretends nothing is passing,
when everything is passing, when the prairie that once held both predator and prey
in some old brutal equilibrium has been unrolled like a rug and shaken out over parking lots,
over subdivisions with names like Elk Meadow and Fox Run that commemorate exactly
what they buried, so that now the hawk hunts a strip of grass beside a highway,
now the coyote trots along a drainage ditch at 2 a.m. because the whole dark continent
of night has been reduced to this culvert, this chain-link, this single lane of desperate hunting—

and I want to hold both of these at once, the killing and the grief for what is killed,
the killing and the larger grief for the whole scaffolding of grass and water and unbroken miles
that made the killing sustainable, that made it something other than a last performance,
because a wolf pulling down a deer in a forest that stretches unbroken to the horizon
is not the same as a wolf pulling down the last deer in a forest that ends at a fence,
though the blood looks the same, though the ribs open the same secret red geography,
though the crows still gather in that same old patient greedy congregation overhead—

so let me praise the fox's silence in tall grass, the owl's face like a clock with no hands,
the shark's whole body a single held breath of intention cutting through blue indifference,
let me praise the teeth, the claws, the talons, the whole terrible competence of hunger,
because it is old, because it is honest, because it does not pretend to be anything
other than what it is, unlike the highway, unlike the plow, unlike the quiet math of extinction
being done in boardrooms far from any field, any tooth, any last shuddering breath—

and let me also grieve, in the same long breath, without contradiction, without apology,
for the passenger pigeon that once darkened the sky for three days straight and does not anymore,
for the buffalo herds that made the earth itself sound like weather, like something arriving,
for every small mouth that will not open again in any field because the field
has become a number in a spreadsheet, has become a name on a map where nothing moves now
except machinery, except the wind finding no wings left to interrupt it—

because awe and grief are not opposites, they are the same animal wearing different weather,
because I can watch the hawk fall and feel my heart lift with it and still know
that the mouse's death matters, that the field's death matters more, that underneath
this whole old animal theater of eating and being eaten there is a newer, quieter violence
erasing the stage itself, and I am standing in the wings of it, applauding, weeping,
unable to look away from either the beauty or the diminishing, because they are,
after all, the same long story, told now in a smaller and smaller room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a reflective poem in the voice of someone returning home after time away, noticing small ecological changes, using eagles as a symbol of resilience amid loss.
counterfactuals.output:
# Coming Back to the River

I know this road by the way it curves
before I see it—muscle memory
older than the years I spent away.
The house still leans a little west.
The dog is different now, but barks
the same warning, welcome bark.

Something's missing that I can't name at first.
Then I count: the maples by the culvert,
three instead of five, and the creek
runs thinner, more transparent,
like it's trying to disappear
politely, without causing a scene.

The old ones mention it in passing—
how June comes early now, how the frost
forgets its schedule, how the geese
seem confused about which way is south.
Small talk, weather talk, the talk
that isn't really about weather.

But this evening, walking the bluff trail
where I used to dare myself toward the edge,
I see them—two eagles, riding a thermal
that shouldn't exist this late in the year,
this high above a river running low.

They don't know what they've survived.
The DDT, the poisoned fish, the guns,
the decades when a man could stand
right here and never see one,
when we'd measured their absence
like a held breath, like a fault we'd carry.

They just ride the warm air rising
off a changing world, indifferent
to the metaphor I'm making of them,
these birds that came back
from the edge of gone
simply because someone decided

they were worth the fight—
the eggshells thick enough again,
the rivers clean enough to hold fish,
the fish enough to hold a life aloft.

I don't know what to do with all this feeling—
homecoming and homesickness
tangled in the same throat,
watching two eagles circle
over water that remembers
being deeper, colder, more itself.

Maybe this is what return means now:
not finding things the same,
but learning to hold two truths
in the same trembling hand—
the loss that keeps accumulating,
quiet as sediment, patient as erosion,

and the eagles, impossibly,
still climbing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem exploring the emotional complexity of loving nature's beauty while acknowledging its violence, set on a clear morning with vivid, breathless syntax.
counterfactuals.output:
# Morning, Unguarded

The light comes in without asking—
gold on the spider's web where something
still struggles, small, its wings
a blur that's slowing, slowing.

I love this hour. I love
the way frost holds the grass blade
like a held breath, the way the hawk
tilts once, a comma in the sky
before it drops—

and I want to look away
and I don't look away
because the field mouse's last warmth
is also morning, also
this particular, unrepeatable light
falling through the particular leaves.

Somewhere a fox is eating something
that was singing an hour ago.
Somewhere the dew doesn't care
what it beads on—thorn or petal,
tooth or open eye.

I keep coming back to this:
the creek doesn't apologize
for what it carries downstream,
the beautiful debris,
the small drowned things
becoming, becoming light
on the water's skin.

How do I hold this—
the way the sun holds
both the blooming and the wilting
in the same unhurried arc,
the way I stand here
grateful, gutted,
watching a world
that would not pause
for my particular grief,

and loving it more for that,
the terrible indifference
dressed in such soft color,
the hawk's wing catching fire
in the same light
that's touching my face now,
tender,
tender,
as if it hadn't just finished
its small, necessary murder—

as if morning were only one thing,
when it is clearly
everything at once:
the web, the wing, the light
that doesn't blink,
the beauty that doesn't
have to ask
permission
to also
be true.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal, confessional poem about place attachment and grief for a lost tree, structured with enjambment and shifting focus between pain and wonder.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Roots Remember

I did not know I loved you
until the chainsaw's whine
threaded through my kitchen window
that Tuesday, ordinary as milk,
and something in my chest
folded like a paper bird
crushed by a careless hand.

Forty years you stood
in the corner of our yard—
before *our* was even a word
my mouth could shape, before
the house was mine to lose sleep over,
you were already old,
already a green cathedral
where light came down
in fractured hymns, already
holding sparrows in your palms
like small brown prayers.

I used to hate the mess of you—
the helicopter seeds
that jammed the gutters,
the roots that cracked
the patio into continents
drifting slowly apart.
I complained. I did not know
complaint was its own
kind of intimacy, the way
you learn to love a person
by cataloging their faults
in the dark, half-asleep,
grateful for the specific weight
of their breathing.

Now the stump sits
like a wound that won't
close into scar, just this
pale circle of rings—
I count them the way
you'd count a life:
here is the drought year,
here is when the ice storm
took your western arm
and you kept growing anyway,
lopsided, generous,
utterly unbothered
by your own asymmetry.

I think grief is just love
with nowhere left to climb.

The sparrows still come back
some mornings, confused,
circling the absence
where a home should be,
and I stand at my window
in my bathrobe, aching
in a language I didn't know
I spoke—this fluency
in loss, this dialect
of dirt and memory,
this strange arithmetic
that says: what shaded me
is gone, and I am still
somehow standing
in the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
